claim: Motor rhythms in many animals originate from networks of central pattern generators (CPGs), neuronal circuits capable of generating rhythmic outputs without rhythmic input.
source: In many animals, motor rhythms originate from networks of central pattern generators (CPGs), neuronal circuits capable of generating rhythmic outputs without rhythmic input (Cohen and Wallen, 1980; Grillner, 2003; Kiehn, 2011; Kristan and Calabrese, 1976; Marder and Calabrese, 1996; Pearce and Friesen, 1984; Yu et al., 1999).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research on CPGs in various animal systems.

claim: CPGs typically generate rhythms through reciprocal inhibitory synaptic interactions between two populations.
source: CPGs typically generate rhythms through reciprocal inhibitory synaptic interactions between two populations.
evidence: This is a statement about established mechanisms of CPG function, drawing on general scientific knowledge.

claim: In vertebrates, motor rhythms arise from half-center oscillator modules in the spinal cord.
source: In vertebrates, motor rhythms arise from half-center oscillator modules in the spinal cord (Marder and Calabrese, 1996).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Marder and Calabrese, 1996.

claim: In the intact animal, sensory feedback plays a critical role in coordinating motor rhythms across the body and modulating their characteristics.
source: Although isolated CPGs can produce outputs in the absence of sensory input, in the intact animal sensory feedback plays a critical role in coordinating motor rhythms across the body and modulating their characteristics (Friesen, 2009; Grillner and Wallén, 2002; Mullins et al., 2011; Pearson, 2004; Wen et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Sensory feedback allows animals to adapt locomotor patterns to their surroundings.
source: Sensory feedback allows animals to adapt locomotor patterns to their surroundings (Andersson et al., 1981; Brodfuehrer and Friesen, 1986) and adapt to unexpected perturbations (Ekeberg and Grillner, 1999).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: In leeches and Drosophila, specialized proprioceptive neurons and sensory receptors in body muscles detect sensory inputs to regulate and coordinate the centrally generated motor patterns.
source: In leeches (Cang et al., 2001; Cang and Friesen, 2000) and Drosophila (Akitake et al., 2015; Mendes et al., 2013), specialized proprioceptive neurons and sensory receptors in body muscles detect sensory inputs to regulate and coordinate the centrally generated motor patterns.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior research on leeches and Drosophila.

claim: In limbed vertebrates, proprioceptors located in muscles, joints, and/or skin detect body movements and interact with premotor interneurons to coordinate limb movements.
source: In limbed vertebrates, proprioceptors located in muscles, joints, and/or skin detect body movements and interact with premotor interneurons to coordinate limb movements (Pearson, 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Pearson, 2004.

claim: Sensory inputs induced by electric stimulation of receptor cells or by mechanical perturbation of body segments can entrain an animal's motor behavior to imposed patterns.
source: Sensory inputs induced by electric stimulation of receptor cells (Yu and Friesen, 2004) or by mechanical perturbation of body segments (Grillner et al., 1981) can entrain an animal's motor behavior to imposed patterns, demonstrating the flexibility of motor systems in responding to feedback.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Efficient locomotion in vertebrates depends on storage of elastic energy in tendons and muscles.
source: Efficient locomotion in vertebrates depends on storage of elastic energy in tendons and muscles (Roberts and Azizi, 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Roberts and Azizi, 2011.

claim: In insects, elasticity in the leg joint plays an important role in generating forces for walking and jumping.
source: In insects, elasticity in the leg joint plays an important role in generating forces for walking and jumping (Ache and Matheson, 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Ache and Matheson, 2013.

claim: C. elegans forward locomotion consists of anterior-to-posterior dorsoventral undulations.
source: C. elegans forward locomotion consists of anterior-to-posterior dorsoventral undulations (Croll, 1971).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Croll, 1971.

claim: C. elegans forward locomotion movements are mediated by a neuromuscular circuit consisting of interneurons, excitatory cholinergic motor neurons, inhibitory GABAergic motor neurons, and body wall muscles.
source: These movements are mediated by a neuromuscular circuit consisting of interneurons, excitatory cholinergic motor neurons, inhibitory GABAergic motor neurons, and body wall muscles.
evidence: This is a statement about the known components of the C. elegans motor circuit, drawing on established knowledge.

claim: The cholinergic B-type motor neurons are required for forward locomotion in C. elegans.
source: Laser ablation studies have shown that the cholinergic B-type motor neurons are required for forward locomotion (Chalfie et al., 1985).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to laser ablation studies by Chalfie et al., 1985.

claim: The GABAergic D-type motor neurons provide dorsoventral cross-inhibition to the body wall muscles and are essential for maintaining normal wave shape and frequency during forward locomotion.
source: The GABAergic D-type motor neurons provide dorsoventral cross-inhibition to the body wall muscles and are essential for maintaining normal wave shape and frequency during forward locomotion (Deng et al., 2021; McIntire et al., 1993).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Deng et al., 2021 and McIntire et al., 1993.

claim: A set of premotor interneurons (AVB, PVC, AVA, AVD, and AVE) regulate forward and reverse movements in C. elegans.
source: A set of premotor interneurons (AVB, PVC, AVA, AVD, and AVE) regulate forward and reverse movements (Chalfie et al., 1988; Driscoll and Kaplan, 1997; Von Stetina et al., 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Ablation of all premotor interneurons or the D-type motor neurons does not deprive C. elegans of the ability to move forward.
source: Ablation of all premotor interneurons or the D-type motor neurons does not deprive C. elegans of the ability to move forward (Chalfie et al., 1985; Gao et al., 2018; Kawano et al., 2011), suggesting that a network consisting of excitatory motor neurons and muscles may be sufficient to generate rhythmicity.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to ablation studies.

claim: A network consisting of excitatory motor neurons and muscles may be sufficient to generate rhythmicity in C. elegans.
source: Ablation of all premotor interneurons or the D-type motor neurons does not deprive C. elegans of the ability to move forward (Chalfie et al., 1985; Gao et al., 2018; Kawano et al., 2011), suggesting that a network consisting of excitatory motor neurons and muscles may be sufficient to generate rhythmicity.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from ablation studies cited.

claim: Multiple oscillators exist in the C. elegans ventral nerve cord.
source: Optogenetic and lesion experiments have shown that multiple oscillators exist in the ventral nerve cord (Fouad et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Fouad et al., 2018.

claim: The mechanisms that give rise to oscillators in the C. elegans ventral nerve cord are still poorly understood.
source: However, the mechanisms that give rise to these oscillators are still poorly understood.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: The B-type motor neurons mediate proprioceptive coupling between anterior to posterior bending during forward locomotion in C. elegans.
source: The B-type motor neurons mediate proprioceptive coupling between anterior to posterior bending during forward locomotion (Wen et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Wen et al., 2012.

claim: The SMDD motor neurons, localized at the head, have been identified as proprioceptive regulators of head steering during locomotion in C. elegans.
source: The SMDD motor neurons, localized at the head, have been identified as proprioceptive regulators of head steering during locomotion (Yeon et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Yeon et al., 2018.

claim: Both the B-type motor neurons and the SMDD head motor neurons have long asynaptic processes hypothesized to have proprioceptive function.
source: Both the B-type motor neurons and the SMDD head motor neurons have long asynaptic processes hypothesized to have proprioceptive function (White et al., 1986) and have been suggested as candidate locomotor CPG elements (Kaplan et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to White et al., 1986 and Kaplan et al., 2020.

claim: The B-type motor neurons and SMDD head motor neurons have been suggested as candidate locomotor CPG elements in C. elegans.
source: Both the B-type motor neurons and the SMDD head motor neurons have long asynaptic processes hypothesized to have proprioceptive function (White et al., 1986) and have been suggested as candidate locomotor CPG elements (Kaplan et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Kaplan et al., 2020.

claim: The cell DVA has been shown to exhibit proprioceptive properties with a dependence on a mechanosensitive channel, TRP-4, which acts as a stretch receptor to regulate the body bend amplitude during locomotion in C. elegans.
source: The cell DVA has been shown to exhibit proprioceptive properties with a dependence on a mechanosensitive channel, TRP-4, which acts as a stretch receptor to regulate the body bend amplitude during locomotion (Li et al., 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Li et al., 2006.

claim: Body bending induces local dendritic calcium transients in PVD and dendritic release of a neuropeptide encoded by nlp-12, which appears to regulate the amplitude of body movements in C. elegans.
source: In another study, body bending was shown to induce local dendritic calcium transients in PVD and dendritic release of a neuropeptide encoded by nlp-12, which appears to regulate the amplitude of body movements (Tao et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Tao et al., 2019.

claim: C. elegans worms displayed a biphasic, sawtooth-shaped phase response curve (PRC) with sharp transitions from phase delay to advance upon transient optogenetic inhibition of the head muscles.
source: We found that the worms displayed a biphasic, sawtooth-shaped PRC with sharp transitions from phase delay to advance.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the experiments described in the manuscript, supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3.

claim: Brief optogenetic inhibition of the head muscles during forward locomotion was followed by a maximum degree of paralysis approximately 0.3 s after the end of the pulse, then a resumption of undulation.
source: Brief inhibition of the head muscles during forward locomotion was followed by a maximum degree of paralysis approximately 0.3 s after the end of the pulse, then a resumption of undulation (Figure 3A,B; Video 1).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the experiments, supported by data shown in Figure 3A,B and Video 1.

claim: The deviation following optogenetic perturbation decays toward zero regardless of the initial deviation from the normal cycle, indicating that the worm tends to return to its normal oscillation after a perturbation.
source: We found that the deviation following optogenetic perturbation (Figure 3—figure supplement 1) decays toward zero regardless of the initial deviation from the normal cycle, indicating that the worm tends to return to its normal oscillation after a perturbation.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the experiments, supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: C. elegans head oscillation during forward locomotion is stable under optogenetic perturbation.
source: These results show that C. elegans head oscillation during forward locomotion is stable under optogenetic perturbation.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data on recovery dynamics after optogenetic perturbation.

claim: During forward locomotion, head oscillation of a worm constitutes a stable oscillator containing a nonsinusoidal limit cycle.
source: Taken together, these results show that during forward locomotion, head oscillation of a worm constitutes a stable oscillator containing a nonsinusoidal limit cycle.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data on phase portraits and recovery dynamics.

claim: Combining the data from all phases of inhibition yielded a sawtooth-shaped PRC with two sharp transitions from phase delay to advance as well as two relatively slow ascending transitions from phase advance to delay.
source: Combining the data from all phases of inhibition yielded a sawtooth-shaped PRC with two sharp transitions from phase delay to advance as well as two relatively slow ascending transitions from phase advance to delay (Figure 3L,M).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the phase response experiments, supported by data shown in Figure 3L,M.

claim: In control worms which do not express NpHR in the body wall muscles, the resulting PRC shows no significant phase shift over any phases of illumination.
source: In control worms, which do not express NpHR in the body wall muscles (see Materials and methods), the resulting PRC shows no significant phase shift over any phases of illumination (Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is a primary finding from control experiments, supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: In worms perturbed with shorter pulses (0.055 s duration), a similar sawtooth-shaped PRC was observed.
source: In worms perturbed with shorter pulses (0.055 s duration), we observed a similar sawtooth-shaped PRC (Figure 3—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is a primary finding from experiments with shorter pulse durations, supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 4.

claim: The sawtooth feature of PRC tends to decrease monotonically as the perturbation occurs further away from the head.
source: We found that the sawtooth feature of PRC tends to decrease monotonically as the perturbation occurs further away from the head (Figure 3—figure supplement 5A,E,I).
evidence: This is a primary finding from experiments with perturbations at different body locations, supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 5.

claim: The sharp decreasing transitions in PRC reflect bimodality in the data rather than continuous transitions.
source: This result shows that the sharp decreasing transitions in PRC reflect bimodality in the data rather than continuous transitions.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the 2-D representation of phase response data.

claim: In transgenic worms expressing NpHR in all cholinergic neurons (Punc-17::NpHR::ECFP), sawtooth-shaped PRCs were observed.
source: In both strains, we again observed sawtooth-shaped PRCs (Figure 3—figure supplements 6 and 7), with variations only in the magnitudes of phase shifts.
evidence: This is a primary finding from experiments with cholinergic neuron inhibition, supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 6.

claim: In transgenic worms expressing NpHR in B-type motor neurons (Pacr-5::Arch-mCherry), sawtooth-shaped PRCs were observed.
source: In both strains, we again observed sawtooth-shaped PRCs (Figure 3—figure supplements 6 and 7), with variations only in the magnitudes of phase shifts.
evidence: This is a primary finding from experiments with B-type motor neuron inhibition, supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 7.

claim: The transient muscle and neuron inhibition interrupt the motor circuit dynamics in a similar manner.
source: These experiments show that the sawtooth-shaped feature of PRC is maintained for motor neuron inhibition, suggesting that the transient muscle and neuron inhibition interrupt the motor circuit dynamics in a similar manner.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the observation that sawtooth-shaped PRCs are observed for both muscle and neuron inhibition.

claim: D-type motor neurons are not necessary for the motor rhythm generator to show the sawtooth-shaped PRC.
source: After performing optogenetic inhibition experiments, we found that the PRC also displays a sawtooth feature (Figure 3—figure supplement 8). This result shows that D-type motor neurons are not necessary for the motor rhythm generator to show the sawtooth-shaped PRC.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from experiments with unc-49(e407) mutants, supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 8.

claim: Sawtooth-shaped PRCs are observed in a number of systems with oscillatory dynamics, including the van der Pol oscillator.
source: Sawtooth-shaped PRCs are observed in a number of systems with oscillatory dynamics, including the van der Pol oscillator (Cestnik and Rosenblum, 2018), and may reflect a phase resetting property of an oscillator with respect to a perturbation (Izhikevich, 2007; Schultheiss et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior research on oscillatory systems.

claim: The net active muscle moment alternates between two plateau regions during forward locomotion in C. elegans.
source: We found that the net active muscle moment alternates between two plateau regions during forward locomotion.
evidence: This is a finding from the analysis of muscle moment patterns, supported by data shown in Figure 2D Inset.

claim: The relaxation oscillator model reproduces the observed PRC.
source: Our model reproduces the observed PRC and describes the locomotory dynamics around optogenetic inhibitions in a manner that closely fits our experimental observations.
evidence: This is a finding from the computational modeling, supported by comparison with experimental data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The relaxation oscillator model describes the locomotory dynamics around optogenetic inhibitions in a manner that closely fits experimental observations.
source: Our model reproduces the observed PRC and describes the locomotory dynamics around optogenetic inhibitions in a manner that closely fits our experimental observations.
evidence: This is a finding from the computational modeling, supported by comparison with experimental data.

claim: The relaxation oscillator model agrees with results on gait adaptation to external load.
source: Our model also agrees with results on gait adaptation to external load and the asymmetry in time-dependent curvature patterns of undulating worms.
evidence: This is a finding from the computational modeling, supported by comparison with experimental data shown in Figure 7.

claim: The relaxation oscillator model agrees with the asymmetry in time-dependent curvature patterns of undulating worms.
source: Our model also agrees with results on gait adaptation to external load and the asymmetry in time-dependent curvature patterns of undulating worms.
evidence: This is a finding from the computational modeling, supported by comparison with experimental data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: The model captures the asymmetric phase portrait trajectory shape found from experiments.
source: We found that in both cases the model result agreed with our experimental observations. Our model captures the asymmetric phase portrait trajectory shape found from our experiments (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is a finding from the computational modeling, supported by comparison with experimental data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The model describes the asymmetry of head bending during locomotion: bending toward the ventral or dorsal directions occurs slower than straightening toward a straight posture during the locomotory cycle.
source: It also describes the asymmetry of head bending during locomotion: bending toward the ventral or dorsal directions occurs slower than straightening toward a straight posture during the locomotory cycle (Figure 4F Inset).
evidence: This is a finding from the computational modeling, supported by comparison with experimental data shown in Figure 4F Inset.

claim: The model provides a simple explanation for the observed bending asymmetry during locomotion.
source: Considering the hypothesized mechanism under the biomechanical background (Equation 1), our model provides a simple explanation for the observed bending asymmetry during locomotion.
evidence: This is a claim about the explanatory power of the model.

claim: The model PRCs consistently exhibited the sawtooth shape found in experiments, although differing in height and timing of the downward transitions.
source: From simulations with different sets of model parameters, we found that the model PRCs consistently exhibited the sawtooth shape found in experiments, although differing in height and timing of the downward transitions.
evidence: This is a finding from the computational modeling simulations.

claim: The threshold-switch mechanism model provides an explanation for the observed sawtooth-shaped PRC.
source: The threshold-switch mechanism model provides an explanation for the observed sawtooth-shaped PRC.
evidence: This is a claim about the explanatory power of the model.

claim: If the effect of the inhibition occurs before the system reaches its switch point, the system will recover by continuing the previous bend and the next switch in the muscle moment will be postponed, thereby leading to a phase delay.
source: (1) If the effect of the inhibition occurs before the system reaches its switch point (Figure 5B), the system will recover by continuing the previous bend and the next switch in the muscle moment will be postponed, thereby leading to a phase delay (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is an explanation of model behavior based on simulations shown in Figure 5B,C.

claim: As the inhibition progressively approaches the switch point, the next switch in the muscle moment will be progressively postponed; this explains the increasing portions of the PRC.
source: (2) As the inhibition progressively approaches the switch point, one would expect that the next switch in the muscle moment will also be progressively postponed; this explains the increasing portions of the PRC.
evidence: This is an explanation of model behavior based on the threshold-switch mechanism.

claim: If the inhibition coincides with the switch point, the muscle moment will be switched at this point and the system will recover by aborting the previous bend tendency, resulting in a small phase advance.
source: (3) If the inhibition coincides with the switch point (Figure 5D), the muscle moment will be switched at this point and the system will recover by aborting the previous bend tendency, resulting in a small phase advance (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is an explanation of model behavior based on simulations shown in Figure 5D,E.

claim: The switching behavior explains the two sharp downward transitions in the PRC.
source: This switching behavior explains the two sharp downward transitions in the PRC.
evidence: This is an explanation of model behavior based on the threshold-switch mechanism.

claim: Model results for frequency and amplitude dependence on viscosity of the external medium are in quantitative agreement with previous experimental results.
source: We found that model results for frequency and amplitude dependence on viscosity of the external medium are in quantitative agreement with previous experimental results (Fang-Yen et al., 2010; Figure 7C,D).
evidence: This is a finding from the computational modeling, supported by comparison with experimental data shown in Figure 7C,D and cited prior research.

claim: Model simulations with three different viscosities produced PRCs with similar sawtooth shape but with sharp transitions delayed in phase as the external viscosity increases.
source: Model simulations with three different viscosities produced PRCs with similar sawtooth shape but with sharp transitions delayed in phase as the external viscosity increases (Figure 7F).
evidence: This is a finding from the computational modeling simulations, supported by data shown in Figure 7F.

claim: The model prediction for how the PRC depends on external viscosity quantitatively agrees with the experimental results.
source: Comparing the relative locations of the transitions in PRCs between the model and the data, our prediction also quantitatively agrees with the experimental results.
evidence: This is a finding from comparing model predictions with experimental data shown in Figure 7G.

claim: The van der Pol oscillator's free-running waveform and phase plot are highly asymmetric, but in an inverted manner compared with the experimental observations.
source: By choosing a set of appropriate parameters, we found that the free-running waveform and phase plot of the van der Pol oscillator are highly asymmetric, but in an inverted manner (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B,F), compared with the experimental observations (Figure 2C,D).
evidence: This is a finding from the computational modeling of the van der Pol oscillator, supported by data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B,F.

claim: Transiently perturbing the van der Pol oscillator with the bell-shaped modulatory function over all phases within a cycle produced a similar sawtooth-shaped PRC as that observed experimentally.
source: Transiently perturbing the system with the bell-shaped modulatory function over all phases within a cycle produced a similar sawtooth-shaped PRC as that observed experimentally (Figure 5—figure supplement 1N).
evidence: This is a finding from the computational modeling of the van der Pol oscillator, supported by data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1N.

claim: The perturbed van der Pol oscillator was found to recover toward its limit cycle with a much slower rate than that of the experiments.
source: However, the perturbed system was found to recover toward its limit cycle with a much slower rate than that of the experiments (Figure 5—figure supplement 1J).
evidence: This is a finding from the computational modeling of the van der Pol oscillator, supported by data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1J.

claim: The Rayleigh oscillator exhibits a highly asymmetric waveform and phase plot that are similar to the experimental observations.
source: From its free-running dynamics, we observed that the system exhibits a highly asymmetric waveform and phase plot that are similar to the experimental observations (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C,G).
evidence: This is a finding from the computational modeling of the Rayleigh oscillator, supported by data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1C,G.

claim: The Rayleigh oscillator produces similar sawtooth-shaped PRCs with respect to transient muscle inhibitions of both sides.
source: Additionally, the Rayleigh oscillator also produces similar sawtooth-shaped PRCs with respect to transient muscle inhibitions of both sides (Figure 5—figure supplement 1O), dorsal side (Figure 6—figure supplement 2C), and ventral side (Figure 6—figure supplement 2G), respectively, and system's recovery rate after the perturbation was shown to be similar to that of the experiments (Figure 5—figure supplement 1K).
evidence: This is a finding from the computational modeling of the Rayleigh oscillator, supported by data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1O.

claim: The Rayleigh oscillator's recovery rate after the perturbation was shown to be similar to that of the experiments.
source: Additionally, the Rayleigh oscillator also produces similar sawtooth-shaped PRCs with respect to transient muscle inhibitions of both sides (Figure 5—figure supplement 1O), dorsal side (Figure 6—figure supplement 2C), and ventral side (Figure 6—figure supplement 2G), respectively, and system's recovery rate after the perturbation was shown to be similar to that of the experiments (Figure 5—figure supplement 1K).
evidence: This is a finding from the computational modeling of the Rayleigh oscillator, supported by data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1K.

claim: The Stuart-Landau oscillator's free-running dynamics show a harmonic oscillation with a sinusoidal waveform.
source: The negative damping of the system constantly neutralize the positive damping on a limit cycle, making its free-running dynamics a harmonic oscillation which shows a sinusoidal waveform (Figure 5—figure supplement 1D,H).
evidence: This is a finding from the computational modeling of the Stuart-Landau oscillator, supported by data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1D,H.

claim: PRCs with respect to transient muscle inhibitions in the Stuart-Landau oscillator are constant with respect to phase.
source: Moreover, PRCs with respect to transient muscle inhibitions are constant with respect to phase (Figure 5—figure supplement 1P), contrary to the experiments.
evidence: This is a finding from the computational modeling of the Stuart-Landau oscillator, supported by data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1P.

claim: Of all the models tested, the threshold-switch model showed the least mean-square error with the PRC data.
source: Of all the models tested, the threshold-switch model showed the least mean-square error with the PRC data (Figure 5—figure supplement 1M–P).
evidence: This is a finding from comparing different models, supported by data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1M–P.

claim: Of the models tested, the threshold-switch model produced the best overall agreement with experiments.
source: We conclude that of these models, our threshold-switch model produced the best overall agreement with experiments.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from comparing different models with experimental data.

claim: Two important experimental findings, the nonsinusoidal free-moving dynamics and the sawtooth-shaped PRCs can be achieved in the threshold-switch model, the van der Pol and Rayleigh oscillators, which are all relaxation oscillators, but not in the Stuart-Landau oscillator, which is not a relaxation oscillator.
source: We also found that two important experimental findings, the nonsinusoidal free-moving dynamics and the sawtooth-shaped PRCs can be achieved in our original model, the van der Pol and Rayleigh oscillators, which are all relaxation oscillators, but not in the Stuart-Landau oscillator, which is not a relaxation oscillator.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from comparing different models with experimental data.

claim: A relaxation oscillation mechanism may underlie C. elegans motor rhythm generation.
source: Taken together, these results are consistent with the idea that a relaxation oscillation mechanism may underlie C. elegans motor rhythm generation.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the modeling and experimental results.

claim: In the model, the mechanism for generating rhythmic patterns can be characterized by a 'relaxation oscillation' process which contains two alternating sub-processes on different time scales: a long relaxation process during which the motor system varies toward an intended state due to its biomechanics under a constant active muscle moment, alternating with a rapid period during which the active muscle moment switches to an opposite state due to a proprioceptive thresholding mechanism.
source: In our model, the mechanism for generating rhythmic patterns can be characterized by a 'relaxation oscillation' process which contains two alternating sub-processes on different time scales: a long relaxation process during which the motor system varies toward an intended state due to its biomechanics under a constant active muscle moment, alternating with a rapid period during which the active muscle moment switches to an opposite state due to a proprioceptive thresholding mechanism.
evidence: This is a description of the model mechanism.

claim: The Fitzhugh-Nagumo model, a prototypical model of excitable neural systems, was originally derived by modifying the van der Pol relaxation oscillator equations.
source: The Fitzhugh-Nagumo model (Fitzhugh, 1961; Nagumo et al., 1962), a prototypical model of excitable neural systems, was originally derived by modifying the van der Pol relaxation oscillator equations.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Fitzhugh, 1961 and Nagumo et al., 1962.

claim: The dynamics exhibited from the action potentials of barnacle muscles in their oscillatory modes were found to yield 'push-pull' relaxation oscillation characteristics.
source: For example, the dynamics exhibited from the action potentials of barnacle muscles in their oscillatory modes were found to yield 'push-pull' relaxation oscillation characteristics (Morris and Lecar, 1981).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Morris and Lecar, 1981.

claim: The beating human heart was found to behave as a relaxation oscillator.
source: The beating human heart was found to behave as a relaxation oscillator (Der pol b, 1940).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Der pol b, 1940.

claim: Several studies of walking behavior in stick insects proposed that the control system for rhythmic step movements constitutes a relaxation oscillator in which the transitions between leg movements is determined by proprioceptive thresholds.
source: Several studies of walking behavior in stick insects (Bässler, 1977; Cruse, 1976; Graham, 1985; Wendler, 1968) proposed that the control system for rhythmic step movements constitutes a relaxation oscillator in which the transitions between leg movements is determined by proprioceptive thresholds.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior research on stick insects.

claim: Head and body motor neurons, including the SMDD head motor neurons and the B-type motor neurons, have proprioceptive capabilities.
source: Previous studies have suggested that head and body motor neurons, including the SMDD head motor neurons and the B-type motor neurons, have proprioceptive capabilities (Wen et al., 2012; Yeon et al., 2018) and may also be involved in locomotory rhythm generation (Fouad et al., 2018; Gao et al., 2018; Kaplan et al., 2020; Xu et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Head and body motor neurons, including the SMDD head motor neurons and the B-type motor neurons, may be involved in locomotory rhythm generation.
source: Previous studies have suggested that head and body motor neurons, including the SMDD head motor neurons and the B-type motor neurons, have proprioceptive capabilities (Wen et al., 2012; Yeon et al., 2018) and may also be involved in locomotory rhythm generation (Fouad et al., 2018; Gao et al., 2018; Kaplan et al., 2020; Xu et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The long undifferentiated processes of cholinergic neurons may function as proprioceptive sensors.
source: This possibility is consistent with earlier hypothesis that the long undifferentiated processes of these cholinergic neurons may function as proprioceptive sensors (White et al., 1986).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to White et al., 1986.

claim: SMDD neurons directly sense head muscle stretch and regulate muscle contractions during oscillatory head bending movements.
source: In particular, recent findings (Yeon et al., 2018) have revealed that SMDD neurons directly sense head muscle stretch and regulate muscle contractions during oscillatory head bending movements.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Yeon et al., 2018.

claim: Many mechanoreceptors are sensitive primarily to time derivatives of mechanical strain rather than strain itself.
source: Many mechanoreceptors are sensitive primarily to time derivatives of mechanical strain rather than strain itself; for example, the C. elegans touch receptor cells exhibit such a dependence (Eastwood et al., 2015; O'Hagan et al., 2005).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The C. elegans touch receptor cells are sensitive primarily to time derivatives of mechanical strain rather than strain itself.
source: Many mechanoreceptors are sensitive primarily to time derivatives of mechanical strain rather than strain itself; for example, the C. elegans touch receptor cells exhibit such a dependence (Eastwood et al., 2015; O'Hagan et al., 2005).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Eastwood et al., 2015 and O'Hagan et al., 2005.

claim: The ability of mechanosensors to sense the rate of change in C. elegans curvature has been proposed in an earlier study.
source: The ability of mechanosensors to sense the rate of change in C. elegans curvature has been proposed in an earlier study (Butler et al., 2015) in which it was hypothesized that the B-type motor neurons might function as a proprioceptive component in this manner.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Butler et al., 2015.

claim: It was hypothesized that the B-type motor neurons might function as a proprioceptive component that senses the rate of change in C. elegans curvature.
source: The ability of mechanosensors to sense the rate of change in C. elegans curvature has been proposed in an earlier study (Butler et al., 2015) in which it was hypothesized that the B-type motor neurons might function as a proprioceptive component in this manner.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Butler et al., 2015.

claim: Mechanosensors encoding a simultaneous combination of deformation and velocity have been observed in mammalian systems including rapidly-adapting (RA) and intermediate-adapting (IA) sensors in the rat dorsal root ganglia.
source: Mechanosensors encoding a simultaneous combination of deformation and velocity have been observed in mammalian systems including rapidly-adapting (RA) and intermediate-adapting (IA) sensors in the rat dorsal root ganglia (Rugiero et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Rugiero et al., 2010.

claim: Proprioceptive feedback that involves a linear combination of muscle length and velocity was suggested by a study of C. elegans muscle dynamics during swimming, crawling, and intermediate forms of locomotion.
source: Proprioceptive feedback that involves a linear combination of muscle length and velocity was also suggested by a study of C. elegans muscle dynamics during swimming, crawling, and intermediate forms of locomotion (Butler et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Butler et al., 2015.

claim: Transiently illuminating dorsal or ventral muscles in the head region of the transgenic worms (Pmyo-3::NpHR) induced a brief paralyzing effect when the segment was bending toward the illuminated side but did not induce a significant paralyzing effect when the segment was bending away from the illuminated side.
source: Transiently illuminating (0.1 s duration) dorsal or ventral muscles in the head region of the transgenic worms (Pmyo-3::NpHR) induced a brief paralyzing effect when the segment was bending toward the illuminated side but did not induce a significant paralyzing effect when the segment was bending away from the illuminated side (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a primary finding from single-side muscle inhibition experiments, supported by data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Both PRCs (dorsal-side and ventral-side illumination) show a peak in the phase range during which the bending side is illuminated but shows no significant phase shift in the other phase range.
source: Combining the experimental data from all phases of dorsal-side or ventral-side inhibition yielded the corresponding PRCs (Figure 6A,B, respectively), from which we found that both PRCs show a peak in the phase range during which the bending side is illuminated but shows no significant phase shift in the other phase range.
evidence: This is a primary finding from single-side muscle inhibition experiments, supported by data shown in Figure 6A,B.

claim: The experimental observations for single-side muscle inhibition are qualitatively consistent with model predictions.
source: The experimental observations are qualitatively consistent with model predictions.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from comparing model predictions with experimental data for single-side muscle inhibition.

claim: The PRC of dorsal-side illumination shows a smaller paralytic response than that of ventral-side illumination.
source: We found that the PRC of dorsal-side illumination shows a smaller paralytic response than that of ventral-side illumination.
evidence: This is a primary finding from comparing PRCs of dorsal-side and ventral-side illumination.

claim: The discrepancy in paralytic response between dorsal-side and ventral-side illumination may be due to different degrees of paralysis achieved during ventral vs. dorsal illumination, possibly due to differences in levels of opsin expression and/or membrane localization.
source: This discrepancy may be due to different degrees of paralysis achieved during ventral vs. dorsal illumination (Figure 6—figure supplement 1), possibly due to differences in levels of opsin expression and/or membrane localization.
evidence: This is a speculation about the cause of the observed discrepancy, supported by data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: C. elegans can swim in water and crawl on moist surfaces, exhibiting different undulatory gaits characterized by different frequency, amplitude, and wavelength.
source: C. elegans can swim in water and crawl on moist surfaces, exhibiting different undulatory gaits characterized by different frequency, amplitude, and wavelength (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is a statement about known C. elegans behavior, supported by data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: Increasing viscosity of the medium induces a continuous transition from a swimming gait to a crawling gait, characterized by a decreasing undulatory frequency.
source: Previous studies Berri et al., 2009; Fang-Yen et al., 2010 have shown that increasing viscosity of the medium induces a continuous transition from a swimming gait to a crawling gait, characterized by a decreasing undulatory frequency (Figure 7C) and an increasing curvature amplitude (Figure 7D).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior research and data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: Increasing viscosity of the medium induces a continuous transition from a swimming gait to a crawling gait, characterized by an increasing curvature amplitude.
source: Previous studies Berri et al., 2009; Fang-Yen et al., 2010 have shown that increasing viscosity of the medium induces a continuous transition from a swimming gait to a crawling gait, characterized by a decreasing undulatory frequency (Figure 7C) and an increasing curvature amplitude (Figure 7D).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior research and data shown in Figure 7D.
